chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Fadalah from al-Ala' from Muhammad from one of them (peace be upon them both): that he was asked about the slave who leads the people in prayer when they are pleased with him and he is the most knowledgeable of them in the Quran, and he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And from him, from Hammad from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slave who leads the people in prayer when they are pleased with him and he is the most knowledgeable of them in the Quran, and he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And from him, from al-Hasan from Zur'ah from Sama'ah, who said: I asked him about the slave who leads the people, and he said, 'Unless he is the most juristically knowledgeable and the most knowledgeable of them.'
And the more precautionary measure is that the slave should not lead in prayer except his own family; he narrated that.

key_terms.أَفْقَهَهُمْ: The most juristically knowledgeable of them
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it

ai.seo_question: Can a slave lead free people in congregational prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding social hierarchy in prayer, prioritizing religious merit (Quranic knowledge and fiqh) over status. While the primary ruling permits a slave to lead free men if they consent and he is superior in knowledge, the *ihtiyat* (precautionary) view restricts this to his own household to avoid potential social friction or diminishment of the leaders' status.
